name: New Business Opportunity Proposal
description: A stage-gated internal venture proposal in midnight navy, warm beige, and cognac orange, covering the market gap, target customer, differentiated solution, investment logic, scenarios, and approval gates.
style_guide:
# New Business Opportunity Proposal

## Purpose

Create an evidence-led internal business opportunity proposal that earns a stage-gate decision. The deck must establish a real market gap, identify the target customer and unmet job, explain the proposed solution and competitive position, quantify the business model and investment, then define learning gates, risks, and the exact approval requested. This is not a fundraising pitch and must not inflate certainty. Preview organizations and figures are fictional.

## Visual signature

Use midnight navy for authority and analytical diagrams, warm beige as the dominant canvas, and cognac orange for opportunity and selected paths. Apply a subtle technical grid only on the cover or one architecture field. Editorial serif headlines pair with compact sans-serif evidence and mono stage-gate labels. Flat panels, thin lines, and sparse geometric connectors create an internal venture-board feel.

## Grid and composition

- Use a fixed 16:9 canvas with `100–120 px` outer margins and 12 columns.
- Reserve `150–185 px` for the section label, conclusion headline, and one-line support.
- Use layouts such as `5/7` evidence split, three customer cards, a `7/5` solution-versus-competition split, or a three-stage gate roadmap.
- Keep beige or white dominant on body pages; navy may fill one large comparison or thesis panel.
- Corners remain square or subtly rounded under `4 px`; no shadows.

## Colors

- Midnight navy `#0A1E3A`: cover, headings, matrix headers, and investment authority.
- Cognac orange `#C86F32`: opportunity marker, selected segment, recommended scenario, and gate numbering.
- Warm beige `#F3EDE2`: dominant canvas.
- White `#FFFFFF`: cards and evidence tables.
- Ink `#182231`: body text.
- Muted taupe `#766D63`: supporting copy.
- Rule beige-gray `#D8D0C4`: dividers.
- Red, green, and amber are reserved for validated risk or decision state, never identity.

## Typography

Use `Georgia` or `Source Serif 4` for opportunity conclusions and major values; `Inter`, `Aptos`, or `Arial` for analysis; `IBM Plex Mono` for stage, source, cohort, assumption, and gate labels. Cover title `54–68 px`; body headline `34–45 px`; hero value `42–56 px`; panel title `19–25 px`; body `13–17 px`; notes `10–12 px`.

## Page archetypes

### 1. Cover and stage-gate context

Use a navy grid field, beige or white title block, and an orange gate marker. Include proposal name, sponsor, stage, review date, requested decision, and confidentiality status. Keep financial claims off the cover.

### 2. Market opportunity and demand drivers

State the market gap as a falsifiable conclusion. Show category size or reachable pool only with method, date, geography, and source. Pair two or three demand drivers with evidence and counter-signals. Distinguish TAM, SAM, SOM, pipeline, and validated willingness to pay.

### 3. Target customers and unmet needs

Use two or three persona or segment fields organized by jobs, pains, gains, buying trigger, economic buyer, user, and evidence. Personas must summarize research, not fictional biographies. Show segment attractiveness and access constraints.

### 4. Proposed solution and competitive position

Explain the minimum solution, value mechanism, and why it wins. Use a capability-to-need mapping plus a compact comparison matrix with consistent criteria. Label unbuilt capabilities, assumptions, and dependencies. Avoid claiming whitespace without verified competitor research.

### 5. Business model, investment, and return

Show pricing or revenue model, unit economics, investment by phase, break-even logic, return range, and base/downside/upside assumptions. Make gross margin, CAC, retention, payback, and cash timing definitions explicit where relevant. Never present a single-point forecast as certainty.

### 6. Stage-gate roadmap, risks, and approval

Use three or four learning gates with hypothesis, test, evidence threshold, spend cap, owner, and stop-or-scale decision. Pair the roadmap with top risks and mitigations. End with a precise approval: amount, capacity, duration, delegated authority, next review, and conditions.

## Evidence and governance

Trace every market, customer, competitive, and financial claim to a source. Separate observed evidence, calculated estimate, benchmark, assumption, and management judgment. Reconcile the requested investment to the roadmap and the return model. Publish kill criteria, not just success criteria. Do not invent customer demand, signed pipeline, regulatory clearance, technical feasibility, or partner commitment.

## Avoid

Do not mimic a startup demo-day pitch, use hockey-stick charts, decorate with generic innovation imagery, conflate interviews with demand, or hide downside cases. Do not claim approval, product readiness, or revenue before evidence exists. Do not crowd the main deck with a full market model; put detailed calculations in an appendix.
